query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The creep resistance of the dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating is primarily governed by the intact FCC/BCC interfaces that act as effective dislocation barriers, impeding dislocation climb and glide under sustained load.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, dual-phase FCC/BCC HEA protective coating exhibiting well-defined, coherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.intervention: Perform high-temperature in-situ TEM or synchrotron X-ray experiments on two sets of specimens: one with the native, intact FCC/BCC interfaces and another with intentionally modified (e.g., roughened or chemically altered) interfaces.
generation.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1000 K, under a constant stress typical of service conditions) that induce creep deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC phase interfaces that serve as barriers for dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under prolonged loading, dislocations are generated and propagate until they meet the FCC/BCC interfaces, which pin them. This pinning delays dislocation motion and reduces effective diffusion paths, leading to lower creep strain rates. Conversely, if the interfaces are modified and lose their coherency, dislocations can bypass these barriers more easily, resulting in accelerated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as-deposited coating with intact interfaces will show observable dislocation pile-ups and periodic pinning at the interfaces with a markedly lower steady-state creep rate compared to coatings with disrupted interfaces. Microstructural observations should reveal less dislocation motion and a slower evolution of creep-induced substructures in the intact-interface specimen relative to the modified one.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited dual-phase FCC/BCC HEA coating with unaltered, coherent interfaces under the same stress and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under sustained creep conditions at elevated temperatures (approximately 1000 K) and mechanical stresses high enough to activate dislocation-mediated plasticity but below the regime where diffusion creep or phase transformations dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies support the role of interfacial barriers in related alloys, the quantitative impact of FCC/BCC interface integrity on creep in HEA coatings is not precisely known, and other factors (e.g., grain-boundary diffusion) may also contribute in varying degrees under different conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of HEA coating specimens: one group retaining the as-deposited FCC/BCC interface structure and another where the interfaces are deliberately disrupted via post-deposition treatments (such as controlled annealing or minor alloying modifications). Subject both groups to identical high-temperature (around 1000 K), constant-stress creep tests while conducting in-situ TEM or synchrotron X-ray measurements to monitor dislocation dynamics and interfacial behavior.
measurements: Real-time observation of dislocation generation, motion, and pinning at FCC/BCC interfaces
Microstructural evolution including any interface degradation or phase transformation
Quantitative measures of dislocation density near the interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the specimens with disrupted interfaces show no significant increase in the creep rate or if in-situ observations fail to demonstrate an association between intact FCC/BCC interfaces and dislocation pinning. Alternatively, if other mechanisms (e.g., grain-boundary diffusion) are observed to dominate the creep behavior regardless of interface integrity, the proposed mechanism is not the primary governing factor.

cited_evidence.text: The preceding analyses clearly indicate that under identical creep conditions, the HESA exhibits a significantly lower creep rate than the HEA, thereby demonstrating superior creep resistance. This section elucidates the underlying reasons for this difference from the perspective of microstructural evolution. Figure 10 presents the creep deformation behavior of HESA under extreme conditions (1000 K and 2.5 GPa), with distinct phase identification via color coding: the γ matrix phase is shown in purple, and the γ′ precipitates are depicted in green. The microstructural evolution reveals continuous dislocation generation at GBs, followed by their subsequent propagation into grain interiors. As creep time progresses, additional slip systems become activated, leading to concurrent dislocation motion within the same grain. This results in the formation of parallel slip bands, which are clearly observed in Figure 10. One of the key features observed is the pronounced hindering effect of the γ/γ′ interface on dislocation motion. A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. decision.trend: Early work (PMC5627260, 2017) on high-entropy superalloys (primarily FCC + ordered precipitates) used elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests to reveal that low stacking-fault energies, high antiphase boundary energies, and stable microstructures enhanced creep strength. Later (PMC8446014, 2021) focused on BCC refractory HEAs, showing that edge dislocations can dominate strength retention at high temperatures, marking a shift toward understanding dislocation-controlled plasticity. Most recently (PMC12842692, 2026) employed molecular dynamics to analyze how stress, temperature, and interfaces affect creep in dual-phase high-entropy superalloys; it highlighted the importance of dislocation mechanisms and phase stability. Despite this progress, the exact role of an FCC/BCC interface in mitigating progressive plastic deformation, under sustained loads, remains largely unsettled.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how the interaction of dislocations with the unique FCC/BCC interfaces under prolonged stress conditions governs creep resistance. Prior studies clarified that controlling factors (stacking-fault energy, precipitates, lattice misfit, and dislocation character) can significantly alter creep. However, direct, time-resolved evidence of how these factors operate within an actual FCC/BCC dual-phase coating under continuous loading is still missing.
decision.lever: Perform high-temperature in-situ TEM or synchrotron X-ray measurements on an as-deposited, dual-phase FCC/BCC HEA coating under sustained stress to track dislocation/interface interactions and emergent substructures in real-time.
decision.why: Previous creep studies of related alloys have emphasized the role of dislocation-based mechanisms but have not captured how dislocations interact with the FCC/BCC interfaces under long-term loading. In-situ tracking will reveal whether interface-dominated dislocation processes—such as climb, pinning, or pile-up at BCC precipitates—govern the alloy’s macroscopic creep response. By comparing microstructural evolution (e.g., dislocation activities, interfacial stability) in baseline vs. interface-modified specimens, one can test the hypothesis that interfacial dislocation barriers control creep resistance. The hypothesis would be falsified if, contrary to expectation, local interface features do not correlate with observed creep properties or if alternate mechanisms (e.g., grain-boundary diffusion) dominate at relevant stresses and temperatures.
